vignette:
Marta Hollenbeck is a 63-year-old sculptor of Polish-American descent who lives with her husband in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. She was referred for psychological assessment following a rape that occurred approximately fourteen months ago, perpetrated by a man she had known for several years - a colleague within the regional arts community who had attended her studio openings, exchanged professional courtesies, and been welcomed into spaces she considered her own. The assault took place in the evening, after a group gathering at a shared studio complex. He had offered to help her carry materials to her car. What followed was violent and prolonged, and it ended with the sound of a distant siren fading into the city noise as she stood alone in the parking structure, unable to move.

In the weeks after the assault, Marta told almost no one. She had gone to a hospital, where she felt processed rather than heard, and when she later attempted to report through formal channels, she encountered what she described - quietly, with a precision that suggested she had rehearsed the words many times - as indifference dressed up as procedure. The detective assigned to her case was dismissive. An arts organization board that became aware of the situation chose to take no action against the perpetrator, citing insufficient evidence. Marta had come to believe, with a certainty that had only hardened over time, that the systems she had trusted throughout her adult life had looked at what happened to her and decided it did not matter enough to act. This conviction sat in her chest like a stone.

The perpetrator remained embedded in the same professional circles. Mutual acquaintances still mentioned his name in conversation, still forwarded his exhibition announcements, still invited both of them - unknowingly, in some cases - to the same events. For Marta, hearing his name, or the names of people connected to him, had become a kind of detonation. She would feel her body flood with something she struggled to name - not quite fear, not quite rage, but a compound of both, shot through with a shame she found bewildering and enraging in equal measure, because she had done nothing wrong and yet the shame arrived anyway, uninvited and insistent. Comments about sexual violence in news coverage, in podcasts, in casual conversation, produced the same response. She had stopped listening to the radio.

The sirens troubled her in a way she found difficult to explain to her husband. They came at night mostly, threading through the neighborhood, and each time one approached she felt the parking structure return to her - not as a memory she was recalling but as something happening again, immediate and physical. She would sit upright in bed, heart loud, scanning the room.

Her studio, which had once been the most alive place in her life, had become difficult. She worked there only in the mornings now, only when her husband was home, and she kept the door to the street visible from her workbench. Unexpected movement - a neighbor appearing suddenly in the doorway, a delivery person rounding the corner of the building - sent a jolt through her that she could not suppress and could not explain away. She had begun to find the work itself hollow. The figures she carved no longer seemed to mean anything. She had always understood her sculpture as a form of reaching toward something - beauty, permanence, the human form held in stone - and that reaching had simply stopped. Nothing she made felt connected to anything larger than the act of making it, and even that felt thin.

She described herself as feeling safe only in her own home, and only in certain rooms of it. She had declined invitations, missed openings, stopped attending the community gatherings that had once anchored her professional and social life. Her husband had grown quietly worried. It was he, finally, who sat with her one evening and said he thought she needed to talk to someone - not because she was broken, he said, but because she deserved more than this. What Marta was most afraid of, she admitted at intake, was that she had already become someone she did not recognize, and that the woman she had been before that evening in the parking structure was simply gone.
